topics.title: SATB format: ranges, spacing, positions
topics.summary: Four voices: soprano and bass are the outer voices, alto and tenor the inner voices. In short score, S and A share the treble staff and T and B the bass staff.
rules: Keep each voice in its range (table).
Spacing: S–A ≤ P8, A–T ≤ P8, T–B ≤ P12.
No voice crossing (exception: alto and tenor may cross briefly).
guidelines: Closed position: no chord tone can be added between soprano and tenor (S–T ≤ P8). Open position: S–T > P8.
Keyboard format: three upper voices in the right hand (close together), bass alone in the left hand.
Stems in short score: soprano and tenor up, alto and bass down.

topics.title: Melodic motion
topics.summary: Each voice should be a good melody. The soprano is the melody line: simple rhythm, mostly chord tones, a clear climax, and tendency tones resolved (7̂ → 1̂).
rules: After a leap of a P4 or larger, change direction.
Leaps larger than an octave are forbidden.
In S, A and T, keep leaps within a 6th (M6).
guidelines: Alto and tenor: mostly conjunct, with repeated notes.
Bass: often disjunct, especially near the end of a phrase.
(Burstein) In every voice avoid leaps of a 7th, augmented intervals (including the A2), and an ascending leap larger than a 3rd into the leading tone.

topics.title: Four types of motion
topics.summary: Between two voices: parallel (same direction, same interval), similar (same direction, different interval), oblique (one voice stays), contrary (opposite directions). Repetition of a chord is not motion. Independence grows from parallel to contrary.
guidelines: The most useful motions are parallel 3rds, 6ths and 10ths.

topics.title: Motion to avoid: parallel, contrary, hidden, unequal
topics.summary: Perfect consonances (P1, P5, P8) are so stable that moving into them in the wrong way removes the independence of the voices.
rules: No parallel P1, P5 or P8 between any two voices.
No consecutive P5 or P8 by contrary motion between any two voices.
No hidden (direct) P5 or P8 between the outer voices: similar motion into a P5/P8 with a leap of a 3rd or more in the soprano. A step in the soprano is acceptable.
No unequal fifths d5 → P5 between any voice and the bass.
guidelines: Find hidden intervals by filling in the leap: the passing notes reveal the hidden parallel.
Hidden 5ths/8ves are softened by more voices, by placing them in inner voices, by a step in the soprano, and by avoiding hidden P8 more than hidden P5 (octaves are more obvious).
P5 → d5 is usually fine; d5 → P5 usually is not.
(Burstein) Never approach a unison by similar motion, and never move into an octave by similar motion from a 2nd or 7th.

topics.title: Complete vs. incomplete chords; 3-part writing
topics.summary: A complete chord contains every chord member. Inverted triads and sevenths are complete. A root-position triad may omit its 5th (triple the root); a root-position seventh chord may omit its 5th (double the root).
rules: Never omit the 3rd or the 7th.
Only the 5th may be omitted.
guidelines: 3-part writing: mostly complete chords; omitting the 5th (R R 3) is allowed depending on the context.

topics.title: Doubling in four parts
topics.summary: Double the most stable chord members. The ear assumes the overtone series: the 5th is the least important member, the 3rd gives the sonority, the root anchors the bass.
rules: Never double the leading tone or a chordal 7th.
guidelines: Exception: in the final chord omit the 5th and triple the root (R R R 3).
Exception: in a deceptive resolution V → vi (VI) double the 3rd of vi.
In instrumental (piano) writing, extra chord "fillers" are allowed.

topics.title: Root-position part writing: procedure and V–I patterns
topics.summary: Connect root-position chords by keeping common tones and moving the other voices the shortest way.
rules: 1. Write the Roman-numeral analysis.
2. Write the chord-tone letter names.
3. Keep common tones (oblique motion in alto and tenor).
4. Move the other voices by step or the smallest leap.

topics.title: First inversion (6/3)
topics.summary: 6/3 chords give the bass line contour and variety, allow smooth parallel 6ths, and are non-cadential. Diminished triads (vii°, ii°) are made stable by inversion: the d5 above the root becomes an M6 above the bass.
rules: 4 parts: any member may be doubled except the leading tone.
3 parts: use complete chords.
Use vii° (and ii° in minor) in first inversion.
guidelines: Parallel 6ths sound "perfect"; a series of 6/3 chords needs careful doubling in four parts to avoid parallel octaves.

topics.title: Second inversion (6/4): passing, neighbour, cadential
topics.summary: The 6/4 is less flexible than the 6/3 because the 4th above the bass is dissonant. Use it only in three ways.
rules: Passing 6/4 (e.g. V6/4 between I and I6): on a weak beat; the bass passes by step.
Neighbour/pedal 6/4 (e.g. IV6/4 over a held I bass): on a weak beat.
Cadential 6/4 (I6/4 → V): on a strong beat.
Approach and leave a 6/4 by step or common tone (a leap into a cadential 6/4 is possible).
Double the bass of a 6/4 (it is the 5th of the root-position chord).

topics.title: Musical structure: phrase to composition
topics.summary: Hierarchy: composition → (movement) → section → (double period) → period → phrase. A phrase is the smallest unit with a complete musical thought (melody, harmony, rhythm), usually closed by a cadence.

topics.title: Cadences
topics.summary: A cadence ends a chord progression and a phrase. Authentic cadences go V → I; half cadences stop on V; deceptive cadences replace I with vi; plagal cadences go IV → I.
rules: PAC: V and I in root position and the soprano moves 2̂ or 7̂ → 1̂.
Conclusiveness (weak → strong): HC, IAC → PAC.

topics.title: Period forms
topics.summary: A period is two (or more) phrases where the first ends weaker (HC or IAC) and the last ends stronger (PAC). Antecedent = question; consequent = answer.

topics.title: Forms: sectional, binary, ternary, sonata, minuet & trio, rondo
topics.summary: Form describes how musical material (melody, tonality) is introduced and repeated at the level of a whole movement.

terms.def: the first section ends on the tonic with an authentic cadence
the first section ends away from the tonic
sections are repeated (written out or with repeat signs)

tables.title: Forms (notes pp.24–26)
rows: two roughly equal sections (symmetrical: same length; asymmetrical: usually B > A); each ≥ 2 phrases. Major: I → V | V → I. Minor: i → III or v | III or v → i
each part is itself binary or simple ternary (nested)

Exposition: 1st theme I – transition (modulation) – 2nd theme V (minor: III or v) – closing theme. Development: modulatory, most tension. Recapitulation: both themes in I (minor: i, or 2nd theme in I or i)

≥ 5 parts; theme A ≥ 3 times, ≥ 2 episodes. Major: I V I (vi/IV/i) I; minor: i (III or v) i (iv or VI) i
